newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK analysts welcome China MFN renewal.
newsitem.headline: HK analysts welcome China MFN renewal.

text.p: Hong Kong's business community on Wednesday welcomed a decisive move in the United States to renew China's trade privileges for another year.
The U.S. House of Representatives voted by a sizeable margin of 259 to 173 to renew China's Most-Favoured Nation (MFN) status, backing President Bill Clinton's decision in May.
Business analysts in Hong Kong saw the move as a confidence booster for the territory, which returns to China on July 1 after more than 150 years of British rule.
"It's great news, the MFN season is always unpredictable," said Mitch Presnick, a partner with Warren Williams International Public Affairs Consultant.
Hong Kong's government, political and business leaders have always pushed for the continuation of China's trade privileges.

The territory estimates it could lose up to US$30 billion annually in trade and related industry revenues if China lost its MFN status. Gross domestic product growth could be cut by about three percentage points and some 86,000 jobs lost. The voting in the United States was closely watched after some conservatives and others in the House said they were preparing for a fight, pointing to China's policies on human and religious rights, trade and other issues.
Some Hong Kong analysts said the large margin could open the way for the United States to start considering granting China permanent trade privileges.

"The vote was overwhelmingly to support President Clinton in renewing China's MFN status. That should be the end of the annual MFN debate as a major exercise," said Bill Overholt, managing director of Asian research at Bankers Trust.
"This should really be the end, The debate now shifts to a debate over whether to grant permanent MFN," he said.
But the renewal failed to inject cheer for some.
"I don't think there is any one person in Hong Kong who even questioned that China would not have its MFN status renewed," said Franklin Lam, director of research at SBC Warburg.
